title: Where Did the Pandemic Hit Hardest? State Unemployment in the CPS, 2019-2026
text:
The question
In the spring of 2020 the U.S. unemployment rate rose more in two months than it did over the entire Great Recession. But a national average hides a lot. A worker in Nebraska and a worker in Nevada lived through very different labor markets. This post asks three questions: how large was the shock nationally, which states were hit hardest and how fast they recovered, and whether a state’s industry mix helps explain the differences.

title: Where Did the Pandemic Hit Hardest? State Unemployment in the CPS, 2019-2026
text:
Data and method
I use IPUMS CPS basic monthly microdata from January 2019 to August 2026, covering about 7.6 million person-month observations of civilians aged 16 and over. Every statistic is weighted with the CPS final person weight (WTFINL), so the numbers describe the U.S. population rather than the raw sample.

Unemployment rate = unemployed / labor force
Labor force participation rate (LFPR) = labor force / civilian population 16+

The series are not seasonally adjusted, so they differ slightly from the BLS headline figures. State estimates are annual averages of monthly data, because single-month samples in small states are noisy. October 2025 is missing because the CPS was not collected during the federal government shutdown, and 2026 covers January to August only.

title: Where Did the Pandemic Hit Hardest? State Unemployment in the CPS, 2019-2026
text:
1. The national shock

Unemployment jumped from 3.8% in February 2020 to 14.5% in April. At the same time, labor force participation fell from 63.4% to 60.1%. That second drop matters: many people who lost jobs stopped looking for work and so were not counted as unemployed at all. The headline unemployment rate therefore understates how much the labor market contracted. By August 2026, unemployment stood at 4.3% and participation at 62.1%.

title: Where Did the Pandemic Hit Hardest? State Unemployment in the CPS, 2019-2026
text:
2. Which states were hit hardest?
The map below shows each state’s annual unemployment rate. Drag the slider or press Play to move through the years, and hover over a state for its unemployment rate, participation rate, and CPS sample size. The color scale is fixed across years, so darker always means higher unemployment.


Code
state_abb <- c(setNames(state.abb, state.name), "District of Columbia" = "DC")

map_df <- state |>
  mutate(code = state_abb[state],
         year_lab = ifelse(YEAR == 2026, "2026*", as.character(YEAR)))

plot_geo(map_df, locationmode = "USA-states") |>
  add_trace(
    type = "choropleth",
    locations = ~code, z = ~ur, frame = ~year_lab,
    zmin = min(map_df$ur), zmax = max(map_df$ur),
    colors = viridisLite::magma(100, direction = -1),
    text = ~sprintf("<b>%s, %s</b><br>Unemployment rate: %.1f%%<br>LFPR: %.1f%%<br>Sample size: %s",
                    state, year_lab, ur * 100, lfpr * 100, format(n, big.mark = ",")),
    hoverinfo = "text",
    marker = list(line = list(color = "white", width = 0.5)),
    colorbar = list(title = "Unemployment<br>rate", tickformat = ".0%")
  ) |>
  layout(geo = list(scope = "usa", projection = list(type = "albers usa"))) |>
  animation_opts(frame = 800, redraw = TRUE) |>
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "Year: ")) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)






The heatmap shows every state and year at once, with states ordered by their 2020 unemployment rate.

Two patterns stand out. First, the shock was highly uneven. Between 2019 and 2020, unemployment rose by 9.3 percentage points in Nevada, 8.8 percentage points in Hawaii, and 6.5 percentage points in Massachusetts, while states in the Great Plains saw much smaller increases. Second, the recovery was fast: by 2022, most states were back close to their 2019 levels.

title: Where Did the Pandemic Hit Hardest? State Unemployment in the CPS, 2019-2026
section: 3. Does industry mix explain the differences?
text:
3. Does industry mix explain the differences?
A natural hypothesis is that states more dependent on in-person services were hit harder, since restaurants, hotels, and entertainment venues shut down first. To test this, I measure each state’s pre-pandemic exposure as the share of its workers employed in leisure and hospitality in 2019.

The relationship is strongly positive, with a correlation of 0.68. But much of this comes from two outliers: Nevada and Hawaii, whose economies depend heavily on tourism. Dropping them, the correlation falls to 0.3. Industry mix still matters, but it is only part of the story. States such as Massachusetts, New Jersey, California, and Michigan had average leisure and hospitality shares yet saw large increases in unemployment. Stricter and longer lockdowns in the Northeast and on the West Coast, and Michigan’s exposure to auto manufacturing shutdowns, are plausible explanations that this data cannot separate.

title: Where Did the Pandemic Hit Hardest? State Unemployment in the CPS, 2019-2026
text:
Takeaway
The COVID-19 labor market shock was national in timing but local in severity. States whose economies relied on tourism and in-person services suffered the largest increases in unemployment, with Nevada and Hawaii as extreme cases. Outside those two states, industry mix explains only a modest part of the variation, which suggests that policy responses and other features of local economies also shaped how hard each state was hit. For policymakers, the lesson is that a single national unemployment rate is a poor guide to where support is most needed during a sector-specific shock.
Code and data: github.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog3-cps. Data source: IPUMS CPS, University of Minnesota, www.ipums.org.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
Intermediate microeconomics hands you a pile of results that look unrelated: Shephard’s Lemma, Hotelling’s Lemma, Roy’s Identity. Each gets its own proof, its own diagram, its own place on the exam.
They are the same theorem. Once you see the envelope theorem, the other three are one-line substitutions.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
The unconstrained case
Let \(f(x,\theta)\) be an objective function and \(\theta\) a parameter. Define the value function
\[V(\theta) = \max_{x} f(x,\theta), \qquad x^*(\theta) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x} f(x,\theta).\]
Substitute the maximiser back in and differentiate by the chain rule:
\[\frac{dV}{d\theta} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\bigg|_{x^*}\frac{dx^*}{d\theta}}_{\text{indirect effect}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\bigg|_{x^*}}_{\text{direct effect}}.\]
At an interior maximum the first-order condition is \(\partial f/\partial x = 0\). The indirect term is therefore zero — no matter how violently \(x^*\) moves. So
\[\boxed{\;\frac{dV}{d\theta} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\bigg|_{x = x^*(\theta)}\;}\]
Note what we never needed: \(dx^*/d\theta\) itself. It is annihilated by the FOC, which is exactly why the theorem is useful when the comparative statics of \(x^*\) are intractable.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
The constrained case
Now impose a constraint:
\[V(\theta) = \max_x f(x,\theta) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad g(x,\theta) = 0,\]
with Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda,\theta) = f(x,\theta) - \lambda\, g(x,\theta)\) and first-order conditions
\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lambda \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}, \qquad g\big(x^*(\theta),\theta\big) = 0.\]
Differentiating \(V(\theta) = f(x^*(\theta),\theta)\) gives the same decomposition as before — but now the indirect term does not vanish, because \(\partial f/\partial x \neq 0\) at a constrained optimum.
The rescue comes from the constraint, which holds identically in \(\theta\). Differentiate it:
\[\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\frac{dx^*}{d\theta} + \frac{\partial g}{\partial \theta} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\frac{dx^*}{d\theta} = -\frac{\partial g}{\partial \theta}.\]
Substitute the FOC \(\partial f/\partial x = \lambda\,\partial g/\partial x\) into the indirect term:
\[\frac{dV}{d\theta} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{dx^*}{d\theta}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}=\lambda\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\frac{dx^*}{d\theta} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} - \lambda\frac{\partial g}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta}\bigg|_{x^*,\,\lambda^*}.\]
Differentiate the Lagrangian, hold \(x\) and \(\lambda\) fixed, done. When \(g\) does not involve \(\theta\), the second term drops out and this reduces to the unconstrained formula. The multiplier earns its keep here: moving \(\theta\) also loosens or tightens the constraint, and that channel is not second-order.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
Four applications
The theorem holds for minimisation too: apply the result above to \(-f\) and negate. Only the second-order conditions differ, and they play no role in the argument.
Shephard’s Lemma. Expenditure minimisation: \(e(p,\bar u) = \min_x \{p \cdot x : u(x) \ge \bar u\}\), so \(\mathcal{L} = p \cdot x - \lambda(u(x) - \bar u)\). Consider \(\theta = p_i\). Then \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial p_i = x_i\), giving
\[\frac{\partial e(p,\bar u)}{\partial p_i} = h_i(p,\bar u).\]
Take \(\theta = \bar u\) instead and \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial \bar u = \lambda\), so \(\partial e/\partial \bar u = \lambda^*\) — the multiplier is the shadow price of utility. The identical argument applied to the firm’s cost function \(c(y,w) = \min_x \{w \cdot x : F(x) \ge y\}\) gives \(\partial c/\partial w_j = x_j(y,w)\), the conditional factor demand.
Hotelling’s Lemma. Profit maximisation over inputs: \(\pi(p,w) = \max_x \{p\,F(x) - w \cdot x\}\), unconstrained. With \(f(x,p,w) = p\,F(x) - w\cdot x\), take \(\theta = p\):
\[\frac{\partial \pi}{\partial p} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\bigg|_{x^*} = F(x^*) = y^*(p,w),\]
the profit-maximising supply. Take \(\theta = w_j\) and \(\partial f/\partial w_j = -x_j\), so \(\partial\pi/\partial w_j = -x_j^*(p,w)\) — the unconditional factor demand.
Roy’s Identity. Utility maximisation: \(v(p,m) = \max_x u(x)\) s.t. \(p\cdot x = m\), so \(\mathcal{L} = u(x) - \lambda(p\cdot x - m)\). Two applications:
\[\frac{\partial v}{\partial p_i} = -\lambda x_i^*, \qquad \frac{\partial v}{\partial m} = \lambda.\]
Divide one by the other and \(\lambda\) cancels:
\[x_i^*(p,m) = -\frac{\partial v/\partial p_i}{\partial v/\partial m}.\]
Marshallian demand recovered from the indirect utility function without solving the consumer’s problem again.
The Le Chatelier principle. Compare a short run with \(x_2\) fixed against a long run where it adjusts. The long-run cost function is the lower envelope of the short-run ones: they are tangent at the reference factor price \(w_1^0\), and \(c^{\mathrm{LR}}\) lies weakly below everywhere else. So \(D(w_1) = c^{\mathrm{SR}} - c^{\mathrm{LR}} \ge 0\) attains its minimum of zero at \(w_1^0\), giving \(D''(w_1^0) \ge 0\). By Shephard, \(x_1 = \partial c/\partial w_1\), so
\[\frac{\partial x_1^{\mathrm{SR}}}{\partial w_1} \ \ge\ \frac{\partial x_1^{\mathrm{LR}}}{\partial w_1}.\]
Both second derivatives are non-positive because cost functions are concave in factor prices — the same envelope argument that makes \(e\) concave in \(p\). Combining this with the inequality above gives, in absolute value,
\[\left|\frac{\partial x_1^{\mathrm{LR}}}{\partial w_1}\right| \ \ge\ \left|\frac{\partial x_1^{\mathrm{SR}}}{\partial w_1}\right|.\]
Long-run conditional demand responds at least as much as short-run. Samuelson’s 1947 result — a consequence of the geometry of optimisation, not of any additional behavioural assumption.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
Why “envelope”?
The name is literal. Fix a consumption bundle \(x^{(k)}\) and ask what it costs as \(p_1\) varies: the answer is \(p \cdot x^{(k)}\), a straight line in \(p_1\) with slope \(x_1^{(k)}\). Every bundle gives one such line.
The expenditure function is the lower envelope of that family — at each price you take whichever bundle is cheapest. A minimum over straight lines is concave, and at every price it is tangent to whichever line is currently optimal. Tangent means equal slope, and that slope is \(x_1^*\). Shephard’s Lemma, read straight off the picture.


Show code
library(ggplot2)

# Cobb-Douglas: u = x1^a * x2^(1-a). All curves below are closed-form
a <- 0.5; u_target <- 1; p2 <- 1

# Expenditure function e(p1,p2,u) = u * (p1/a)^a * (p2/(1-a))^(1-a)
e_true <- function(p1) u_target * (p1/a)^a * (p2/(1-a))^(1-a)

# Hicksian demand for good 1, from Shephard: h1 = a*e/p1
h1 <- function(p1) a * e_true(p1) / p1

p_grid <- seq(0.5, 4, length.out = 200)

# Cost of the bundle that was optimal at p0, evaluated at every p1
fixed_bundle_line <- function(p0) {
  x1 <- h1(p0)
  x2 <- (1 - a) * e_true(p0) / p2
  data.frame(p1 = p_grid, cost = p_grid * x1 + p2 * x2, anchor = p0)
}

lines_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.75, 1.25, 2, 3), fixed_bundle_line))
env_df   <- data.frame(p1 = p_grid, cost = e_true(p_grid))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = lines_df, aes(p1, cost, group = anchor),
            colour = "grey65", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = env_df, aes(p1, cost), linewidth = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 6)) +
  labs(x = expression(p[1]), y = "Expenditure") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Figure 1: Grey lines: the cost of holding one fixed bundle as \(p_1\) varies. Black curve: the cost of re-optimising at every price. The black curve is their lower envelope, and grazes each line tangentially.





Each grey line is a consumer who never adjusts. The black curve is one who re-optimises constantly. Where they touch, they graze — the gap opens quadratically, not linearly. That is the envelope theorem as a picture: at the optimum, small adjustments are free to first order.
Data. No external data. Every curve is generated from the closed-form Cobb-Douglas expenditure function in the code above; the only inputs are \(a = 0.5\), \(\bar u = 1\), \(p_2 = 1\).

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
Takeaway
When you differentiate a value function, ignore how the optimal choice moves and differentiate the Lagrangian directly. That single fact gives you Shephard, Hotelling, Roy and Le Chatelier — plus the reason a small tax has deadweight loss proportional to the square of the tax. Four lemmas, one theorem, and the FOC doing all the work.

title: Are NBA Salaries Efficient? Scraping Stats and Contracts to Find Mispriced Players
text:
The question
Under the salary cap, every dollar a team spends on one player is a dollar it can’t spend on another. So the useful question for a front office is not who the best players are, but who delivers the most production per dollar. If salaries tracked on-court value closely, there would be no bargains to find. This post tests that: I scrape a full season of player statistics and salaries, estimate what the league pays for production, and measure how far each player sits from that rate.

title: Are NBA Salaries Efficient? Scraping Stats and Contracts to Find Mispriced Players
Are NBA Salaries Efficient? Scraping Stats and Contracts to Find Mispriced Players
text:
Method
Production is measured by VORP (value over replacement player), a box-score estimate of a player’s total contribution above a freely available replacement.
To get a market rate, I regress log salary on VORP using only players aged 25 and over. Most of them signed their current deals in free agency, while many younger players are on rookie-scale contracts whose pay is set by draft position rather than negotiated. Applying this curve to every player gives a market value: roughly what a veteran with the same production earns. Surplus value is market value minus actual salary. Predictions are converted back to dollars with Duan’s smearing estimator and capped at the league’s highest salary, since no contract can exceed the max.

title: Are NBA Salaries Efficient? Scraping Stats and Contracts to Find Mispriced Players

title: Are NBA Salaries Efficient? Scraping Stats and Contracts to Find Mispriced Players
section: What a front office should do with this
text:
What a front office should do with this
First, surplus is concentrated in rookie-scale contracts, which makes draft picks the cheapest source of production in the league. A team trying to contend should value its picks accordingly and plan its window around when those players are still on rookie deals.
Second, the biggest overpayments are long contracts that run into players’ 30s. The age premium means teams are still paying for past performance, so shorter terms or declining salary structures reduce that risk.
Third, the undrafted and second-round group is the one source of surplus not created by rookie-scale rules. Scouting outside the lottery for productive players on minimum deals is where a disciplined team can still find value that other teams miss.

title: Are NBA Salaries Efficient? Scraping Stats and Contracts to Find Mispriced Players
text:
Limitations
VORP accumulates with playing time, and teams may give expensive players more minutes than their performance warrants; Staw and Hoang (1995) found this kind of sunk-cost effect for draft position in the NBA. That inflates the measured production of expensive players, so the surplus of cheap players is probably understated. Age is also only a proxy for contract type, and a single season is a noisy sample.

title: Are NBA Salaries Efficient? Scraping Stats and Contracts to Find Mispriced Players
text:
Takeaway
NBA salaries follow current production only loosely, and the gap is systematic: the league underpays young players because rookie contracts are fixed by rule, and overpays veterans for what they used to do. For a team working under a fixed cap, the cheapest wins are the ones it drafts or finds outside the first round.

panel <- read_csv(paste0(base, "data/processed/g7_panel.csv"))

# Look up one number: measure m, year y, column uk / peer / gap
val <- function(m, y, col = "gap") gap[[col]][gap$measure == m & gap$year == y]
f1  <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", abs(x))

yr_gdp   <- max(gap$year[gap$measure == "gdp_pc_idx"])
yr_other <- max(gap$year[gap$measure == "invest_chg"])

# Largest GDP shortfall between the financial crisis and the referendum
pre <- gap |>
  filter(measure == "gdp_pc_idx", year >= 2008, year <= 2015) |>
  slice_min(gap, n = 1)

# Where the UK ranks among the seven on growth since 2016
rank_uk <- panel |>
  filter(year == yr_gdp) |>
  mutate(rank = rank(-gdp_pc_idx)) |>
  filter(iso2c == "GB") |>
  pull(rank)

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
text:
The question
In June 2016 the UK voted to leave the European Union. It formally left in January 2020 and exited the single market and customs union at the end of that year. Ten years after the vote, economists still disagree about what it cost. The difficulty is that we never observe the UK that stayed.
This post takes a simple approach to that problem. I compare the UK with the other six G7 economies, before and after the referendum, on three measures where Brexit should show up if it mattered: output, investment, and trade. If the UK tracked its peers before 2016 and fell behind afterwards, that is evidence consistent with a Brexit cost. If it did not, the simple story needs rethinking.

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
text:
Data and method
The data come from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators, downloaded with the WDI package in R for the seven G7 countries from 2000 to 2025. I use three indicators:

Real GDP per capita (NY.GDP.PCAP.KD, constant 2015 US dollars)
Gross fixed capital formation as a share of GDP (NE.GDI.FTOT.ZS)
Trade, exports plus imports, as a share of GDP (NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS)

Raw levels are not comparable across these countries, so each series is transformed before plotting.

GDP is measured per capita and in real terms, then indexed to 2016 = 100. Per capita matters because population growth differs across the G7, and indexing puts every country on the same scale in the referendum year.
Investment and trade shares are shown as the change in percentage points since 2016. Germany trades a far larger share of its GDP than the United States does, so comparing levels would mostly show country size. Comparing changes shows who moved.

The comparison group is the unweighted average of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United States. I keep only years in which all seven countries report data, so the average never changes composition. This is why investment and trade end in 2024.
This is a descriptive comparison and not a causal estimate. The G7 average stands in for what might have happened to the UK without Brexit, and the limitations section discusses how well it does that job.

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
section: 1. Output: a gap that opened after exit, not after the vote
text:
1. Output: a gap that opened after exit, not after the vote

The referendum itself left no visible mark on output. In 2019, three years after the vote, the UK index stood at 104.3 against 104.1 for its peers.
The gap appears in 2020. The UK’s pandemic recession was deeper, leaving it 4.8 points behind. It recovered part of that ground by 2022, when the gap narrowed to 1.4 points, and then fell back again. In 2025 real GDP per capita was 5.5% above its 2016 level in the UK and 9.0% above in the peer group, a shortfall of 3.4 points. Among the seven countries, the UK ranks 5 out of 7 for growth since 2016.
Is a gap of that size unusual? Not by itself. Because every country is set to 100 in 2016, the chart also shows relative growth before the referendum: between 2011 and 2016 the UK outgrew its peers by 3.2 points. Swings of this size have happened before, in the UK’s favour. What stands out now is the direction and the persistence: the shortfall was 3.1 points in 2023, 3.6 in 2024, and 3.4 in 2025, well after pandemic restrictions ended.

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
text:
2. Investment: a recovery that stalled

Investment is where economists expected the referendum to bite first, because firms facing uncertainty about future market access tend to postpone spending. The data fit that story, with a caveat.
By 2024 the peer group’s investment share was 1.4 percentage points above its 2016 level. The UK’s was 0.1 points above, essentially unchanged. A gap was already visible in 2019 (0.6 points) and has stayed between 1 and 2 points since 2020.
The caveat is that the two lines were far from parallel before 2016. UK investment had been climbing out of a deep post-crisis trough: its share of GDP rose 2.4 points between 2011 and 2016 while the peer average was flat. The honest reading is that UK investment did not fall after the referendum. A recovery stopped, at the moment when investment in comparable economies began to rise. Note also that this indicator covers all fixed investment, including housing and government, and not business investment alone.

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
text:
3. Trade: the weakest evidence

Trade should give the cleanest test, since leaving the single market raised trade barriers on a known date. The timing does line up. Through 2019 the UK’s trade share had risen faster than its peers’, by 2.7 points, plausibly because the fall in sterling after the referendum raised the pound value of both imports and exports. In 2021, the first year outside the single market, the gap flipped to 3.1 points behind, and it was 1.8 points behind in 2024.
But the UK series is volatile, and that undermines the result. In 2015, before any of this, the UK was already 4.2 points below the peer average on the same measure. The post-2021 gap sits inside the range of gaps seen before the referendum. The direction is what a Brexit effect would predict, but on annual trade shares I cannot distinguish it from ordinary noise. The spike in 2022 across both lines likely reflects energy prices, which raise the nominal value of imports everywhere.

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
text:
Explore the data
The chart below combines the three measures. Use the buttons to switch between them, hover over any year to see the size of the gap, and drag the slider at the bottom to zoom in on a period.


Code
col_uk   <- "#C8102E"
col_peer <- "#1F3A5F"

measures <- c(
  gdp_pc_idx = "Real GDP per capita (2016 = 100)",
  invest_chg = "Investment share of GDP (pp change since 2016)",
  trade_chg  = "Trade share of GDP (pp change since 2016)"
)
button_labels <- c("GDP per capita", "Investment", "Trade")
events <- data.frame(year  = c(2016, 2021),
                     label = c("Referendum", "Leaves single market"))

p <- plot_ly()
for (i in seq_along(measures)) {
  d <- filter(gap, measure == names(measures)[i])
  p <- p |>
    add_trace(
      x = d$year, y = d$peer, type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
      name = "G7 average (ex-UK)", visible = (i == 1),
      line = list(color = col_peer, dash = "dash", width = 2),
      hovertemplate = "G7 avg: %{y:.1f}<extra></extra>"
    ) |>
    add_trace(
      x = d$year, y = d$uk, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers",
      name = "United Kingdom", visible = (i == 1),
      line = list(color = col_uk, width = 3),
      marker = list(color = col_uk, size = 5),
      fill = "tonexty", fillcolor = "rgba(200,16,46,0.12)",
      text = sprintf("%+.1f", d$gap),
      hovertemplate = "UK: %{y:.1f}<br>Gap vs peers: %{text}<extra></extra>"
    )
}

buttons <- lapply(seq_along(measures), function(i) {
  vis <- rep(FALSE, 2 * length(measures))
  vis[c(2 * i - 1, 2 * i)] <- TRUE
  list(method = "update", label = button_labels[i],
       args = list(list(visible = vis),
                   list("yaxis.title.text" = measures[[i]])))
})

vlines <- lapply(events$year, function(x) {
  list(type = "line", x0 = x, x1 = x, yref = "paper", y0 = 0, y1 = 1,
       line = list(color = "grey", dash = "dot", width = 1))
})

annots <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(events)), function(i) {
  list(x = events$year[i], y = c(1, 0.93)[i], yref = "paper",
       text = events$label[i], showarrow = FALSE,
       xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top",
       font = list(size = 11, color = "grey"))
})

p |>
  layout(
    hovermode = "x unified",
    margin    = list(t = 60),
    xaxis     = list(title = "", rangeslider = list(visible = TRUE)),
    yaxis     = list(title = measures[[1]]),
    shapes    = vlines,
    annotations = annots,
    legend    = list(orientation = "h", x = 1, xanchor = "right",
                     y = 1.03, yanchor = "bottom"),
    updatemenus = list(list(
      type = "buttons", direction = "right",
      x = 0, y = 1.03, xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
      buttons = buttons
    ))
  ) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
text:
Limitations

Other shocks hit at the same time. The UK left the single market in the middle of a pandemic and one year before an energy crisis to which its gas-dependent economy was especially exposed. A comparison with peers cannot separate these from Brexit.
The G7 average is an imperfect counterfactual. The investment and trade charts show that the UK did not move in parallel with its peers before 2016, so some of the later divergence may have happened anyway. A synthetic control that weights countries to match the UK’s pre-2016 path would be the natural next step.
Annual data hide timing. Events such as the referendum in June and the end of the transition period in December fall inside single observations.
Trade shares are nominal. They move with exchange rates and commodity prices as well as with trade volumes.

title: Did Brexit Leave the UK Behind? Output, Investment, and Trade Against the G7
text:
Takeaway
Three charts give three different strengths of answer. Output gives the clearest signal: the UK kept pace with the G7 for three years after the referendum, then fell about 3 points behind after it actually left and has not recovered the ground. A swing of similar size, in the UK’s favour, occurred in the five years before the referendum, so this alone is not proof. Investment points the same way, as a recovery that stalled while peers’ investment rose. Trade does not settle anything at this level of aggregation.
The broader lesson is about timing. The damage many expected from the vote itself does not appear in output. What the data show is a slower divergence that began once the new trading arrangements took effect, which is also when it became hardest to tell apart from everything else that went wrong in 2020.
Code and data: github.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog4-brexit. Data source: World Bank, World Development Indicators.
